continuities.name: Arthur Conan Doyle canon
continuities.description: The four novels and five short-story collections by Arthur Conan Doyle (the 60 canonical stories).
continuities.quote: Traditionally, the canon of Sherlock Holmes consists of the 56 short stories and four novels written by the British writer and physician Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.
continuities.notes: In-universe years only where the novel/collection article states them; collections span many years and are placed relatively. Baring-Gould dates were not used (not stated in these articles).

continuities.name: Basil Rathbone films (1939-1946)
continuities.description: 14 films with Basil Rathbone and Nigel Bruce: two Victorian-set Fox films, then twelve Universal films updated to the then-present Second World War era.
continuities.quote: A series of fourteen films based on Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories was released between 1939 and 1946; the British actors Basil Rathbone and Nigel Bruce played Holmes and Dr. John Watson, respectively. The two films from Fox had large budgets, high production values and were set in the Victorian era.
continuities.notes: One continuity per the series article (same leads, recurring Mrs Hudson/Lestrade), although Fox vs Universal changed the era. Possible branch split fox/universal.

continuities.name: Granada Sherlock Holmes (Jeremy Brett, 1984-1994)
continuities.description: Granada Television adaptations for ITV, four named series.
continuities.quote: Sherlock Holmes is the overall title given to the series of Sherlock Holmes adaptations produced by the British television company Granada Television between 24 April 1984 and 11 April 1994.

continuities.name: Sherlock (BBC, 2010-2017)
continuities.description: Moffat/Gatiss contemporary adaptation, four series plus the Victorian-set special The Abominable Bride.
continuities.quote: The series is set in the present day. The one-off special features a Victorian-period fantasy resembling the original Holmes stories. Sherlock is a mystery crime drama television series that presents a contemporary adaptation of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes detective stories.

continuities.name: Elementary (CBS, 2012-2019)
continuities.description: CBS contemporary update set in New York City.
continuities.quote: Elementary is an American procedural comedy-drama television series that presented a contemporary update of Arthur Conan Doyle's character Sherlock Holmes. The series was set and filmed primarily in New York City.

continuities.name: Guy Ritchie films (2009-2011)
continuities.description: Warner Bros. films with Robert Downey Jr. and Jude Law.
continuities.quote: In 1891, a series of bombings blamed on political radicals bring France and Germany to the brink of war.
continuities.notes: Separate adaptation; the sequel continues the 2009 film.

titles.title: Sherlock Holmes and the Voice of Terror

units.label: Film
units.release_quote: Film sequence table, Release column for Sherlock Holmes and the Voice of Terror: {{dts|format=dmy|1942|September|18}}

in_universe.label: Second World War era (then-present, 1942)
in_universe.quote: In February 1942, following negotiations with the Doyle estate, Universal Pictures acquired the rights to the films and signed contracts with Rathbone and Bruce to continue their portrayals.{{sfn|Davies|1976|p=69}} Universal's deal—worth $300,000—was for seven years, and they purchased the rights to 21 stories in the canon in a contract that stipulated that the company had to make three films a year, of which two had to be adaptations of Doyle's stories.{{sfn|Barnes|2011|pp=214–15}} Universal was allowed to substantially revise the adaptations and modernise them,{{sfn|Boström|2018|p=241}} often to the point where little of the original story remained recognisable.{{sfn|Boström|2018|p=242}} Universal decided to update the stories to a Second World War setting, and the first film, Sherlock Holmes and the Voice of Terror—based on Doyle's 1917 story "His Last Bow"—was updated to a Second World War setting, with Holmes attempting to capture a Nazi agent.{{sfn|Langman|Finn|1995b|pp=250–51}} Rathbone and Bruce both initially objected to updating the setting of the stories.{{sfn|Boström|2018|p=242}} The change of era for Holmes is explained in the opening titles, with a caption that informs viewers that Holmes is "ageless, invincible and unchanging", going on to say that he was "solving significant problems of the present day".{{sfn|Voice of Terror|2003}}
in_universe.note: No source gives a story year: the setting is contemporary with its release, which is not the same as a stated year, so it is ordered by release.

in_universe.quote: In February 1942, following negotiations with the Doyle estate, Universal Pictures acquired the rights to the films and signed contracts with Rathbone and Bruce to continue their portrayals.{{sfn|Davies|1976|p=69}} Universal's deal—worth $300,000—was for seven years, and they purchased the rights to 21 stories in the canon in a contract that stipulated that the company had to make three films a year, of which two had to be adaptations of Doyle's stories.{{sfn|Barnes|2011|pp=214–15}} Universal was allowed to substantially revise the adaptations and modernise them,{{sfn|Boström|2018|p=241}} often to the point where little of the original story remained recognisable.{{sfn|Boström|2018|p=242}} Universal decided to update the stories to a Second World War setting, and the first film, Sherlock Holmes and the Voice of Terror—based on Doyle's 1917 story "His Last Bow"—was updated to a Second World War setting, with Holmes attempting to capture a Nazi agent.{{sfn|Langman|Finn|1995b|pp=250–51}} Rathbone and Bruce both initially objected to updating the setting of the stories.{{sfn|Boström|2018|p=242}} The change of era for Holmes is explained in the opening titles, with a caption that informs viewers that Holmes is "ageless, invincible and unchanging", going on to say that he was "solving significant problems of the present day".{{sfn|Voice of Terror|2003}}
